item.research_question: How can colloidal high-entropy alloy (HEA) nanoparticles with targeted equimolar stoichiometry and diameters below 5 nm be synthesized in a single step, and can this process be scaled for industrial application?
item.processing_route: Single-step liquid-phase, ultrashort-pulsed laser ablation of consolidated and heat-treated micropowders of the five constituent metals; low-power system: 10 ps Nd:YAG laser, 1064 nm, 100 kHz, 8.8 W, ethanol solvent, 20 mL min⁻¹ flow; high-power system: 3 ps laser, 1030 nm, 10 MHz, water solvent, 500 mL min⁻¹ flow, scanning speed 484 m s⁻¹
item.test_conditions: Electrochemical analysis in 0.1 M NaOH (pH 13) using a three-electrode setup with Pt counter electrode and Ag/AgCl reference; potentials corrected to RHE; linear sweep voltammetry at 20 mV s⁻¹ with electrode rotation at 1600 rpm; current densities extracted at 1.7 V vs. RHE
key_findings: Colloidal HEA nanoparticles with diameters less than 5 nm were successfully synthesized, with ultrasmall NPs (2.8 nm) making up the main product by number, surface, and volume.
The process demonstrated unprecedented scalability with a productivity of 3 grams of colloidal HEA nanoparticles per hour using the high-power laser system.
The chemical composition of the nanoparticles was nearly equimolar, preserving the target stoichiometry without selective ablation of single elements.
The crystal lattice of the nanoparticles was preserved as a single fcc structure, matching the bulk HEA target, as confirmed by XRD, SAED, and HRTEM.
The synthesized nanoparticles exhibited unique redox behavior in an alkaline environment, with mass activities of 0.104 A mg⁻¹ at 1.7 V vs. RHE for water-based synthesis.
Surface segregation of Cr and Mn was observed in larger NPs (>50 nm) due to longer residence times in the low-density mixing region, leading to minor spinel oxide formation.
The synthesis process was highly reproducible, with variations of less than 10% in productivity and size distribution, and up to 12% deviation in catalytic performance.
item.mechanism: The formation mechanism involves laser irradiation creating a plume and cavitation bubble; ablated species mix with liquid vapor in a supercritical state, cool rapidly (cooling rates ~10¹² K s⁻¹), and condense into NPs. Ultrasmall NPs form via nucleation and condensation in the low-density mixing region, while larger NPs emerge from a molten layer due to Rayleigh–Taylor instability. Surface segregation and oxidation occur in a late stage for larger NPs with longer residence times, while smaller NPs cool too fast for segregation.
item.limitations: The presence of a minor spinel oxide phase and surface segregation of Cr and Mn in larger NPs; the complexity of assigning specific redox features to individual metals in the multi-element system; and the lack of direct quantitative surface analysis (e.g., XPS) to confirm surface compositions.
item.future_work: The authors propose varying the composition of the CoCrFeMnNi alloy to identify the most active composition for catalysis, extending quantitative and structural analysis of NP surfaces to investigate the origin of catalytic performance, and utilizing the method for rapid screening of different functional materials by varying alloy composition, liquid environment, and immobilization substrate.
quotes: Herein, this study reports the single-step synthesis of colloidal CoCrFeMnNi HEA nanoparticles with targeted equimolar stoichiometry and diameters less than 5 nm by liquid-phase, ultrashort-pulsed laser ablation of the consolidated and heat-treated micropowders of the five constituent metals.
Further, the scalability of the process with an unprecedented productivity of 3 grams of colloidal HEA nanoparticles per hour is demonstrated.
Cooling rates of the condensates in the order of 10¹² K s−1 can be expected, and passivation of the surface of the NPs that occurs by the interaction with solvent species suppresses further growth.
